data.title: GM's CEO succession plan could include tech-savvy executive -- Bloomberg
data.description:
The search for a successor to Mary Barra at General Motors could focus on someone with technical expertise and deep knowledge of self-driving technology, putting GM’s chief product officer Sterling Anderson as a top contender for the chief executive job.

According to Bloomberg, Anderson has met with board members for one-on-one meetings, although the purpose of these meetings is unconfirmed.

The company has reportedly begun searching for Barra’s successor, preparing for whenever she steps down from the role she has held since 2014.

While GM’s recent move to the Nasdaq exchange means the company is no longer mandated to have a succession plan, the GM board is aware that as Barra approaches her 65th birthday on December 24, the time has come to have her replacement in place.

According to Bloomberg, Anderson is the frontrunner, but the company is also reportedly considering CFO Paul Jacobson and GM President Mark Reuss, as well as outside candidates recommended by executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles.

Seidman holds voting and investment authority over the shares reported by the group through his roles at the firms and their general partner.

Trump weighs fresh Iran strikes as Centcom warns of force strain - report
data.description:
President Donald Trump is facing growing pressure from hawkish U.S. officials and Israeli leaders to restart joint military strikes on Iran, as U.S. Central Command warns that a sustained deployment beyond December threatens to erode military readiness, according to a media report published Friday.

Centcom has briefed administration officials that the toll on forces from maintaining the military build-up past year-end could compromise readiness, the Financial Times reported, citing three people familiar with the matter, including U.S. officials.

One source told the FT that Centcom is telling the administration it is "running out of time, burning money and readiness," including the capacity to address other global threats, with the large deployment against Iran nearing a full year.

Military planners are also eyeing an incoming Democratic-led Congress likely to curtail defense spending and tighten oversight of the war. A U.S. military official disputed the characterization, the FT reported, saying it was not true that Centcom was warning forces would become overextended if strikes were not renewed before the new year.

Israeli officials have seized on the shrinking window argument. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu—serving after an inconclusive election—has warned repeatedly of "great threats" from Iran and claimed without evidence that Tehran is pushing to restart its nuclear program,the FT reported. Mossad chief Roman Gofman traveled to Washington last week for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe in a bid to "provide information and persuade" the Trump administration to renew joint strikes. Israel's security establishment is also reportedly discussing a smaller operation if broad joint action fails to materialize.

Trump, however, has appeared reluctant to commit, telling Axios on Thursday he was not "rushing into any decision" and would "see what happens after the beginning of the year." The president has oscillated between threats and calls for diplomacy, more recently saying he is content with the status quo—a naval blockade on Iran.

data.title: Ford, Honda, Stellantis, VW sue New Jersey to block 'extortionate' vehicle repair law
data.description:
By Jonathan Stempel

Ford , Honda , Stellantis' FCA unit and Volkswagen sued New Jersey on Friday to block a new state law they say increases the amounts automakers must pay franchised dealers for warranty and recall repairs.

In a complaint filed in federal court in Trenton, New Jersey, the automakers said the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Open Recall Notice and Fair Compensation Act gives dealers a "blank check" to set prices for warranty, recall and other repair services, while prohibiting manufacturers from avoiding "extortionate" results or recovering the costs.

New Jersey's law will shift more than $375 million a year to dealers from automakers, giving dealers a "windfall" by imposing no obligation to use the money to improve customer service or boost compensation for employees, the automakers said.

"In short, the act rewards dealers for charging their customers more," the automakers said.

The office of New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, who enforces the state's laws, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

New Jersey's law took effect on April 1, after former Governor Phil Murphy signed it in September 2025.

CONSTITUTIONAL VIOLATIONS ALLEGED

The automakers objected to letting dealers charge a "labor multiplier" based on samples of repair orders, saying it lets dealers bill for substantially more labor time than they actually work.

They also challenged provisions requiring automakers to pay marked-up prices on parts that the dealers received at reduced cost or for free, and preventing automakers from providing less expensive parts even if supply, demand or other factors justified price cuts.

Ford, Honda, FCA — which includes Fiat and Chrysler — and Volkswagen said that since the law took effect, each has received dozens of bills requiring payment "for hours that no technician works, that surpass what comparable dealers charge for the same work, and that exceed what retail customers pay."

They said the law violates the US Constitution's Commerce Clause and Takings Clause, is preempted by federal law governing recalls, and violates New Jersey's Constitution.

The nonprofit New Jersey Coalition of Automotive Retailers is also a defendant. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

  • WEC does not currently anticipate an impairment from the capital-cost disallowance, except for about $1.7 million in unrecovered depreciation expense.

data.title: Cattle Futures Rise Ahead of Feedlot Report — Market Talk
data.description: Live cattle futures rose for a third consecutive session as the market awaited the USDA's monthly Cattle on Feed report. Cattle and calves on feed totaled 11.6 million head as of Nov. 1, down 1% from a year before. Placements on feedlots in October fell 7% from the year-earlier month to 1.89 million head, the lowest for the month on records back to 1996. Marketings of fed cattle at 1.62 million head were also a record low for October, and down 5% on the year. "Monthly Cattle on Feed reports have repeatedly shown tighter than expected supply in recent months, but the subsequent optimism has typically not lasted long with heavy selling pressure clouding not just the cattle complex, but broader livestock/protein sector as a whole," Mike Castle of StoneX says in a note. Live cattle settled up 0.1% on CME at $2.23 a pound ahead of the report. Hogs edge up 0.3% to 52.6 cents a pound. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

data.title: Citi closes long sugar call with stop-loss, keeps bullish outlook
data.description:
Citi closed its long sugar call position with July expiry (SBN7C) on Friday at a loss of 47 cents, after a stop-loss signal was triggered, the bank said in a note.

  • Active fund selling intensified, driven by a weaker Brazilian real , Citi said, adding that it may be exiting near the lower end of the recent trading range.

  • The bank left its quarterly price outlook unchanged, saying its constructive view on sugar remains intact.

  • Recent price action has been driving by market volatility and Brazilian currency weakness, according to Citi.

  • Raw sugar prices fell nearly 5% on Thursday and lost 7.5% this week.

  • Citi continues to expect lower supply from India due to El Niño, and sees potential limits on how much extra sugar Brazil can send to global markets.

  • The recent sell-off has been excessive relative to fundamentals and could offer an attractive entry point for medium-term investors, Citi said.

data.title: Niron Magnetics to build $1.8 billion Alabama rare-earth-free magnet facilty
data.description:
Niron Magnetics said on Friday it will build a $1.8 billion rare-earth-free permanent magnet manufacturing campus in Dothan, Alabama, as the company expands domestic capacity and strengthens US supply chains.

The Alabama facility will be the company's second manufacturing plant. Niron expects to open its first full-scale plant in Minnesota in 2027, with a capacity of up to 1,500 metric tons annually.

  • Construction is expected to begin in 2028, with production starting in 2029 and reaching an annual production capacity of 10,000 metric tons

  • The project is expected to create 700 high-wage jobs within five years

  • Niron said its iron nitride magnets do not rely on rare earth elements, offering an alternative to conventional neodymium magnets

  • The Minneapolis-based company said its magnets are used in artificial intelligence infrastructure, automotive, defense, industrial and consumer electronics applications

  • Washington has been seeking to increase domestic output of critical minerals and reduce reliance on China, which dominates the global rare-earths supply chain

data.title: CBOT wheat ends lower in range-bound trade
data.description:
Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures closed lower in range-bound trade on Friday, pressured by a lack of supportive news as well as a surge in the dollar this month that has made US grains less competitive globally, traders said.

  • CBOT December soft red winter wheat settled down 4 cents at $5.74-1/4 per bushel and most-active March wheat ended down 3 cents at $5.92, one day after falling to $5.81-3/4, its lowest level since mid-January.

  • Both contracts stayed inside of their respective trading ranges from Thursday.

  • K.C. March hard red winter wheat (KWH27) ended down 1/4 cent on Friday at $6.40-1/4 a bushel and Minneapolis March spring wheat (MWEH27) fell 3-1/4 cents to finish at $6.38-1/4 a bushel.

  • The dollar index eased slightly on Friday after rallying to 19-month highs this week on mounting expectations for US interest rate hikes. The strong US currency has created broad pressure on dollar-denominated commodities.

  • Grain traders continues to monitor escalating hostilities in the Black Sea export region. Russia launched one of the largest missile and drone attacks of the war on Ukraine on Friday, after President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian attacks on a bridge to Crimea.

  • Argentina's 2026/27 wheat harvest is progressing with yields above expectations, the Buenos Aires grains exchange said on Thursday, estimating the crop at 23.4 million tons, the country's second-highest production.

data.title: New AI Releases Help Google Avoid Worst of Tech Rout — WSJ
data.description:
By Erin Woo

Few were spared in Friday's tech rout, but Alphabet shares held up better than its Silicon Valley peers. Shares of the Google parent closed 2.7%, lower compared with a 5.3% drop for the Nasdaq index.

Google announced two new AI releases this week: Gemini 4 Neon, a new mid-size frontier model, and Tasks in Gemini, new personal assistant features in its chatbot app. "Neon seems to be a banger!" Elon Musk said in a post on X about the release.

Josh Beck, an analyst with Raymond James, said that it was important that Google was closing the gap with the AI-model frontier. "They already had somewhat of a challenging report, and then a few glimmers of hope in the last couple weeks," Beck said.

But, Beck said, whether Google is able to monetize AI search will be the biggest factor in Google's stock price over the next several months.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).
